# `ghost_in_runtime`: a ghost value used by the running program

A ghost parameter (`ghost s : T`), a `ghost let` and a `ghost fn` exist only for proofs: the
compiler removes them before the program runs. So the program itself may not use one. A ghost
value may appear only where nothing runs:
- in a refinement, such as a parameter's or the result's;
- in another `ghost let`, or as the argument of a ghost parameter;
- as a lemma's argument, or in a proof hint (`assert … by`, `calc`);
- in a `ghost fn`'s body.

Returning it, branching or matching on it, capturing it in a closure, passing it to an
ordinary parameter, or calling a `ghost fn` from ordinary code is this error.

## A program that triggers it

```march
mod Main do
  fn clamp(x : Int, ghost limit : Int) : Int do
    if x > limit do limit else x end
  end
end
```

## The fix

If the program needs the value, it is not ghost: make it an ordinary parameter.

```march
mod Main do
  fn clamp(x : Int, limit : Int) : Int do
    if x > limit do limit else x end
  end
end
```

If only the proof needs it, keep it ghost and use it in the contract instead:

```march
mod Main do
  fn below(ghost limit : Int, x : {Int | _ < limit}) : {Int | _ < limit} do
    x
  end
end
```

## Why the rule exists

Erasing ghost code must not change what the program does. If a branch, a result or a closure
could depend on a ghost value, removing it would leave the program reading something that no
longer exists, or would change its behaviour. Keeping ghost values out of every runtime position
makes erasure safe by construction.

See also: [the lemmas guide](../lemmas.md#ghost-code-proof-only-parameters-bindings-and-functions), `ghost_misuse`.
